note: The adaptive spelling journey across the eight inflection rules (EN.FND.SPL.inflections). Lessons, hints and mistake explanations are provisional: written for OpenPath from the existing lessons (lessons.json) and the doubling journey, not yet reviewed by an educator. The words come from content/english/spelling/journey-words.json (built by tools/english/spelling/build_journey_bank.py). Hint templates use {base}, {ending}, {word}, {last} and {stem}; the last hint level of every strategy is a worked example that shows the answer and is recorded as such. Mistake explanations are shown only when the typed answer is exactly the misspelling the rule predicts; any other wrong answer gets a neutral explanation that names no misconception.

plain.skill: Adding -s, -ed and -ing with no change (look → looking, kick → kicked)

strategies.name: Rule and examples

lesson.title: Just add the ending
steps: Most words just take the ending.
The base word does not change: look → looks, looked, looking.
lesson.tip: Say the base word first, then add the ending you hear.

hints: Write {base} first, exactly as it is.
Now add {ending} to the end. Nothing else changes.

strategies.name: Build the word in parts

lesson.title: Two parts
steps: Part 1: the base word (paint).
Part 2: the ending (-ing).
Put them together: paint + ing = painting.
lesson.tip: Check: can you still see the whole base word?

hints: Keep every letter of {base}, then add {ending}.

es_plural.skill: Adding -es after s, x, z, ch and sh (box → boxes), and plain -s elsewhere (book → books)

strategies.name: Rule and examples

lesson.title: When to write -es
steps: Words ending in s, x, z, ch or sh add -es.
You can hear the extra syllable: fox → foxes, catch → catches.
Other words just add -s: book → books.
lesson.tip: If you can hear an extra 'iz' sound at the end, write -es.

hints: Look at the last letters of {base}. Is it s, x, z, ch or sh?
Say it: can you hear an extra 'iz' at the end?

strategies.name: Listen for the extra syllable

lesson.title: Count the beats
steps: Clap the base word: box (1 beat).
Clap the new word: box-es (2 beats).
An extra beat means -es. No extra beat means -s.
lesson.tip: The extra beat needs the e to make a sound.

hints: An extra beat after {base}? Then you need -es.

mistakes.s_not_es: {base} ends in a hissing sound (s, x, z, ch or sh), so it takes -es: {word}.
mistakes.es_after_other_ending: {base} does not end in s, x, z, ch or sh, so it just takes -s: {word}.

double_short.skill: Doubling the last consonant of short words (hop → hopping, big → bigger), and not doubling when there are two letters (jump → jumping)

mistakes.no_doubling: {base} ends in one short vowel and one consonant, so the {last} doubles: {word}.
mistakes.over_doubling: {base} does not end in one vowel and one consonant, so nothing doubles: {word}.

drop_e.skill: Dropping the silent e before -ing (make → making), but keeping ee, ye and oe (agree → agreeing)

strategies.name: Rule and examples

lesson.title: Dropping the silent e
steps: Does the word end in a silent e? (make, ride)
Drop the e before -ing: make → making.
But keep ee, ye and oe: agree → agreeing, see → seeing.
lesson.tip: The i in -ing does the e's job, so the e is not needed.

hints: Does {base} end in a silent e?
Take the e off, then add the ending: {stem} + {ending}.
Worked example (this shows the answer): {base} without its e is {stem}; {stem} + {ending} = {word}.

lesson.title: Swap the e for the ending
steps: Write the base word: hope.
Rub out the silent e: hop_.
Add the ending: hoping.
lesson.tip: Only the silent e goes. A double ee stays: free → freeing.

mistakes.kept_silent_e: {base} ends in a silent e. It goes before -ing: {word}.
mistakes.dropped_needed_e: {base} ends in ee, ye or oe, which stays: {word}.

y_to_i.skill: Changing y to i after a consonant (carry → carried, happy → happier), but keeping it before -ing and after a vowel (crying, played)

strategies.name: Rule and examples

lesson.title: Changing y to i
steps: Does the word end in a consonant + y? (carry, happy)
Change the y to i before -ed, -er, -est or -es: carried, happier, ladies.
Keep the y before -ing (crying) and after a vowel (play → played).

examples.note: a vowel before the y: keep it

lesson.tip: Never two i's together: cry → crying, not criing.

hints: Look at the letter before the y in {base}. Vowel or consonant?
A consonant before the y: change y to i, unless the ending is -ing.

strategies.name: Sort first

lesson.title: Sort, then spell
steps: Sort: vowel + y (play, enjoy) or consonant + y (carry, try)?
Vowel + y: just add the ending.
Consonant + y: y becomes i, except before -ing.
lesson.tip: Two quick questions: what is before the y, and is the ending -ing?

hints: Sort {base}: vowel + y, or consonant + y?
Now check the ending: is it -ing?

mistakes.y_not_changed: {base} ends in a consonant + y, so the y changes to i: {word}.
mistakes.changed_y_wrongly: Here the y stays (a vowel before it, or the ending is -ing): {word}.

stress_doubling.skill: Doubling in longer words stressed at the end (begin → beginning, admit → admitted)

strategies.name: Rule and examples

lesson.title: Listen for the strong beat
steps: Say the word and find the strongest syllable.
Strong beat at the END and one vowel + one consonant? Double: be-GIN → beginning.
Strong beat at the START? Do not double: VIS-it → visited.
lesson.tip: Say the word aloud and listen for which syllable is strongest.

hints: The strong beat is at the end, so the {last} doubles.

strategies.name: Clap the beat

lesson.title: Clap and spell
steps: Clap the word, making the strong syllable loud.
Loud clap last? The last letter doubles.
Loud clap first? Just add the ending.
lesson.tip: Compare preFER → preferred with OFfer → offered.

hints: Clap {base}. Loud clap first or last?

mistakes.no_doubling: {base} is stressed at the end, so the {last} doubles: {word}.
mistakes.over_doubling: {base} is stressed at the start, so nothing doubles: {word}.

no_double_unstressed.skill: Not doubling when the stress is earlier (visit → visited, open → opening)

strategies.name: Rule and examples

lesson.title: When not to double
steps: Say the word and find the strongest syllable.
Strong beat at the START? Do not double: OP-en → opening.
Strong beat at the END? Double: be-GIN → beginning.
lesson.tip: Compare: preFER → preferred, but OFfer → offered.

hints: The strong beat is at the start, so nothing doubles.

strategies.name: Clap the beat

lesson.title: Clap and spell
steps: Clap the word, making the strong syllable loud.
Loud clap first? Just add the ending.
Loud clap last? The last letter doubles.
lesson.tip: Most two-syllable words are loud at the start, and most do not double.

hints: Clap {base}. Loud clap first or last?

mistakes.over_doubling: {base} is stressed at the start, so nothing doubles: {word}.
mistakes.no_doubling: {base} is stressed at the end, so the {last} doubles: {word}.

exceptions.skill: Tricky endings: ie to y (die → dying), adding k after c (panic → panicked), British -ll- after one vowel (travel → travelled) but not after two (reveal → revealed)

strategies.name: Rule and examples

lesson.title: Three tricky patterns
steps: ie becomes y before -ing: die → dying.
Add k after a final c: panic → panicked.
In British spelling, a final l after ONE vowel doubles: travel → travelled. After TWO vowels it does not: reveal → revealed.
lesson.tip: OpenPath teaches British spelling, and also accepts American spellings as correct.

hints: Which tricky pattern does {base} have: ie, c, or l?
Use that pattern's change, then add {ending}.

lesson.title: Fix the end, then add
steps: Find the tricky end: ie, c or l.
Fix it: ie → y, c → ck, and l → ll only after one vowel.
Add the ending.
lesson.tip: Without the k, panicing would say 'pan-i-sing'.

mistakes.missing_k: Words ending in c add a k before -ed or -ing, so the c keeps its hard sound: {word}.
mistakes.no_doubling: In British spelling, the final l doubles: {word}. (The American spelling with one l is also accepted.)
mistakes.over_doubling: {base} has two vowels before the l, so the l does not double: {word}.

slip: So close: two letters swapped. The word is {word}.
